utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm told that all the redactions are done and it's now just the uploading into e-court process, which takes a while, but it will definitely be done by the end of the week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We thank you all for your cooperation, and we can now move to Mr. Ostojic. You have nothing else to add, Mr. Zivanovic, have you?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd just like to apologise to you because yesterday I was over-stepped my time allocated by the Trial Chamber. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Right. As you and everyone else knows, we are very patient, because -- at least I don't speak for myself only. I speak also on behalf of my colleagues. We all learned of the virtue of patience as being one of the most important things a Judge ought to have. But, on the other hand, we expect basic courtesy. I'm not attacking you, but we expect basic courtesy, and also your colleagues ought to know whether they've got to start today or whether they're going to start tomorrow. But so, anyway, leave it. Thank you for your words, and we will now proceed with Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ostojic, just give me one second. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Fair and thorough are two concepts that we expect in every trial. It is fundamentally the standard that must be strictly adhered to in such an extraordinary and significant case that is before this honourable Trial Chamber. My name is John Ostojic, and along with Mr. Predrag Nikolic and our Defence team, we represent Ljubisa Beara. The OTP in this case, in its preparatory comments, has shared with the Court that it's been a privilege to appear before you, and we certainly incorporate their comments. And without going into more detail, we certainly want to thank the entire staff, the translators, court reporters, as well as Ms. Stewart, who has assisted us with some documents throughout this case. It has been a long journey, and it is coming to an end for us. For the Court, as you know, it is the beginning of the process of your deliberation. We view the evidence differently than the Prosecution, and we hope during these closing remarks we can enlighten or share with you our precise view, which the Prosecution has either ignored or simply failed to comprehend. We are not contentious because we want to be. We are contentious because we believe that they've used and adopted certain evidence and manipulated that evidence in order to fit a theory, a theory of "one size fits all," a theory that they, in their initial statement in August of 2006, said that they do not believe in collective guilt. But when you truly look at their evidence, you will find that that is their theory, "one size fits all," that every Serb who is in the VRS should be found guilty. We ask that this Court look at the evidence, as it will, and we're very confident that you will clearly, and dissect it as you would both the Prosecution's case as well as the Defence case. The OTP has remarkably weaved half-truths, uncorroborated and contradictory, inconsistent statements of biased witnesses, with unreliable and tainted documents, in a futile attempt to establish that Ljubisa Beara was purportedly involved in the crimes alleged in the indictment. In order to test the worthiness of the OTP's case, I respectfully submit that a practical and pragmatic approach is required, and not a fanciful, "one size fits all" approach used by the Prosecution. I do believe that the Prosecution was not fair, and I do believe that the Prosecution was not thorough in the presentation of their evidence. And what do we mean when we say "not fair"? I suggest to the Court that they ignored evidence, although it is their duty, not ours, to present evidence to this Trial Chamber. They have the burden of proof. Which evidence, in short, did they ignore. Milos Tomovic, for example, the driver of Ljubisa Beara, an individual that they interviewed, an individual that we tried to get his statement introduced into evidence and were respectfully rejected. What other evidence did they ignore? We heard from Ms. Soljan that there's no evidence of 1.500 to 3.000 Bosnian men from a column being killed through legitimate combat engagements, land-mines, or suicides. How could they ignore the evidence of an independent source, such as Edward Joseph's report at Exhibit 1D374? Why do they ignore that evidence? How could they, after hearing that evidence and testimony, not address it or reconcile it? Further, on the issue of the column, they ignore completely not only the independent evidence of Mr. Joseph, but they ignore the evidence of their own investigator, Dusan Janc, who explained, I believe, during his cross-examination where the legitimate combat engagements occurred and what his estimates were as to the number of people that perished from those legitimate combat engagements. They give you a fanciful argument that there were some surface remains, and that's the extent that they'd like to share with us. So they ignore the independent evidence of the United Nations, an individual who was at the scene and on the site. They ignore their own investigator. But more importantly, they ignore the victims. The evidence that we introduced in connection with this case also were statements from people who were actually within the column. The Bosnian Muslim men who walked through Susnjari and made it through Tuzla or Kladanj, they've given evidence in this case, and they've said at certain instances, We found that there were 500 dead bodies as a result of this combat engagement, 1.000 in another instance, 1500 at another location. How could they ignore the evidence? Well, they do simply because it doesn't fit within their theory. Why do they ignore the evidence? Because they persisted in a theory that simply is inaccurate. And in my view, they're trying to manipulate those facts. They talk about some and only a few of our Defence witnesses, and we're still talking about ignoring evidence. They don't address Mr. Jakov Bienenfeld. He was brought here to share with you the intent of Mr. Beara, how he is as a man, how he is as a person, how he is as a colleague, how he interacted with a different ethnic group. Mr. Bienenfeld was clear and precise in what he said about Mr. Beara. They simply ignore it. Further, and perhaps most importantly, they ignore the evidence of 2D PW-19. He was a Bosnian Muslim and brought here for the same reason, to share with the Court what Mr. Beara's intent may be, how his relations were with other ethnic groups. Their position is quite simple: Ignore anything and everything that may assist an accused or may be helpful. Mr. McCloskey promised us certain things throughout this case, both in his opening statement and most recently in his closing argument. He said, I stick by my word. What I say in court is what I mean. He told us again last week that if there are two reasonable interpretations, that the Court is required to accept the interpretation in favour of the Defence. Yet throughout this case, when you view any piece of evidence, they never view it with the Defence in mind. They have a narrow view of the evidence and have adapted it, and adopt only their version. I strongly believe that the Prosecution was not fair because they also distorted the evidence. Look simply at Exhibit 7D-2D642. That is what we've called the Croat intercept, and I'm not still certain why it's given both the 7D and the 2D number, but that's what I'm told that it is, so it's 642. Look at the date of it, July 13th. Look at the timing of it, 11.25. The Prosecution is the one, when I brought this evidence to him, that told me it was exculpatory. Now their position is, as reflected in their brief, that it's deliberately deceptive, that Mr. Beara was cunning in some of his actions. So that we understand their position, if there is any favourable or exculpatory evidence against the accused, all they can say is that they were cunning, they lied, or they were deliberately deceptive. Mr. Vanderpuye, and I apologise for mentioning him because he's not in our presence, but I'm sure watching, challenged us on this exhibit. He tells the Court, in his closing remarks, The Defence should have looked where the document came from. The Defence should have found out the source. The Defence should have determined who the speakers were in the conversation with respect to this document. With all due respect, that is not our job, and it is the job of the Prosecution, who claims that they want the truth to be heard. They seised this evidence. They had the capacity and the manpower to answer all those questions from Mr. Vanderpuye. We want that evidence to be heard, we want to know who was on that tape, and we want to know who the source was of those comments. You'll find it's interesting that the Prosecution, on one hand, finds it exculpatory, but, on another, claims that it's deceptive, deliberately deceptive. As Mr. Vanderpuye says, Those two cannot coexist. You cannot have it both ways. When we talk about manipulation of the evidence, I was a bit surprised to see the Prosecution relying on some witnesses, in fact witnesses that they've called liars, and corroborating their evidence with other witnesses that they've called liars. That also cannot coexist. We've also seen --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We've also seen the Prosecution rely on evidence by an individual and then use self-corroboration to claim to the Court that that's sufficient and carries the burden of proof beyond a reasonable doubt. For example, if I were a witness and I wrote down that I witnessed something, or reflect upon it, can I use my own document as corroboration or is that just one factor that you would utilise? The Prosecution has no corroborating evidence in this case as it relates to Ljubisa Beara, and I will walk you through that evidence with time permitted. They tell you, in a nutshell, that they prefer quantity over quality. They claim that they have 14 witnesses that saw Mr. Beara from the 10th through the 16th of July, and that ten of those witnesses purportedly saw him on the 13th and 14th of July, 1995. I suggest to the Court to look at the quality of those witnesses as opposed to the quantity of those witnesses. We will, with all due respect, go through, hopefully, each one of those rather briefly. The Prosecution has, from time to time, argued that they have consistent evidence of certain facts, but that's not the standard. They must prove it conclusively, beyond a reasonable doubt. When we speak of standards, I can't help but recall what Mr. Vanderpuye said the other day with respect to Mr. Beara's witnesses. That's not the standard, Mr. Vanderpuye. Mr. Vanderpuye and the Prosecution, in my view, have a double standard. Their standard is that if a young man comes in and testifies in court, and makes a mistake as to when handball practice started, you should dismiss that testimony. The Prosecution also believes that if a woman comes into court and she remembers details about someone's clothing, you should respectfully dismiss that testimony. What this Court knows, and I apologise for having to remind you, is that the same standards should be used, and the hypocrisy in the Prosecution is that they argue that witnesses like Milan Kerkez and Svetlana Gavrilovic either did not have enough detail or were overly detailed and you should dismiss them. If they use their own standard and approached it against their own witnesses, none of them, absolutely none of them, would pass muster and would not be allowed to testify in this case. That's the hypocrisy and their evaluation of our evidence. They ignore like Mr. Bienenfeld and 2D PW-19, and yet they distort the evidence of other witnesses such as Milan Kerkez and Svetlana Gavrilovic. I think they also manipulate the evidence, with all due respect. They talk about a person by the name of Bosko Momcilovic, that he claims that he saw Ljubisa Beara on the 10th or 11th of July in the IKM in Pribicevac. Look at that evidence, as we will, and you will find that that is not accurate, it is not precise, it is not worthy of you giving any credence to it. It is as Mr. Vanderpuye said, "valueless."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I suggest for the record, because it's missing in line 8 of the transcript, Bosko --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Momcilovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Momcilovic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The OTP claims that Beara did not always wear glasses, and they've tried to show Professor Wagenaar a video of Beara's voluntary surrender to The Hague. We saw, within that video, when Mr. Beara was meeting with the minister, I believe, that the glasses were in his pocket. We tried to view whether there were any markings on the bridge of his nose. There is absolutely no evidence at all that Mr. Beara ever failed to wear his glasses during the day or evening, except when he slept. Likewise, I think the Prosecution wasn't fair when they failed to keep their word. They told us from the beginning of the case, all the way through the close of the Prosecution case, when we gave our submissions, and they acknowledged that they called Mr. Beara an empty vessel, but they said, We have evidence that Mladic gave him orders. We can link it up. They don't. No such evidence exists with respect to contacts or orders or correspondence or reports between Mr. Beara and General Mladic. I've been advised -- with the Court's permission, if I can go into closed or private session for one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of course. Let's go into private session for a short while, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, we are in open session, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It's actually --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The Prosecution also told us that Ljubisa Beara was an empty vessel, but that wasn't all he said last Friday. He also told us, as you remember, in the opening statements he used an idiom, and that is that Ljubisa Beara "cannot hold a candle to Blagojevic," or any other commanders. They're required to explain what they said at that trial and to show you that their taking a consistent view. They've not explained why they called Mr. Beara an empty vessel or why they used the idiom that he cannot hold a candle to any of the commanders. Thoroughness. I think the Prosecution knows that during the cross-examination of various witnesses, we tried to show the Court that they were not thorough or complete in some of their evaluation, whether it was their methodology, whether it was the materials they used, or the analysis that they provided. That completeness is necessary in all criminal proceedings, in my view, if the standard of proof is beyond a reasonable doubt. We tell the Court they failed to call relevant, critical, and necessary evidence. It's perhaps naive to think that someone can make that charge and not be able to substantiate it. The Prosecution, in my view, does it. The Defence is restricted. But when I tell this honourable Chamber that they failed to call relevant, critical, and necessary evidence, I'm referring to Nova Kasaba, July 14th, 1995. I am referring to Mr. Egbers. As everyone knows, the evidence purportedly that occurred that day was not as it was with many of their 14 witnesses, one-on-one with Mr. Beara, although in open no one else observed them. This meeting with Mr. Egbers was between at least four individuals who were supposedly present, according to Mr. Egbers. Zoran Malinic was present. Why didn't the Prosecution call him as a witness? Do they have doubt about what he may say? The Prosecution listed Zoran Malinic in their 65 ter list. The Prosecution knows that the 65 ter list is inconsistent with what is written in Mr. Malinic's interview statement. They have the obligation, if they want to corroborate the evidence and show the Court beyond a reasonable doubt that Mr. Beara was purportedly present at Nova Kasaba, to at the very least call Zoran Malinic. Of course, they'll give you their same excuse, All Serbs are liars, you can't trust those people who were involved in this war. Why don't they call the interpreter, Nebojsa, who was neutral? He was there. They had access to him, interviewed him, met with them. Their investigators clearly could have convinced him or asked or had him even subpoenaed to come here. But forget about Zoran Malinic and the interpreter Nebojsa. They could have went two hours away from The Hague, and I think the town is Assen, and I may have mispronounced it. They could have got Egbers' former colleague in DutchBat, Theo Lutke. They interviewed him, they had statements from him. It's their obligation to bring forth that evidence if they believe that they can prove that Mr. Beara was present beyond reasonable doubt. The fact that they did not bring such evidence forward, in my view, suggests that there is doubt as to his presence. Specifically given the testimony of the various Defence witnesses, there is little question but that there is doubt as to Mr. Beara's presence on that date. Finally, with respect to thoroughness and fairness, I'd like to say that the Prosecution, not only in applying their standard with respect to Defence witnesses, that they have a double standard, but they have a double standard as to even interpretation of words. By way of example, we can look at the Vasic documents, P60, P62, P886. Here's a person who acknowledges and admits his involvement in certain portions of the war. The dates of these documents are not only relevant, but are on point as to the entirety of the Prosecution's case, the 12th and 13th of July. Here's a person who uses the word "liquidation" or "killing" in his July 13th report, P886, and yet the Prosecution tells you, with a straight face, He really didn't mean 'killing,' he was exaggerating the fact that MUP was solely involved to his bosses. He was exaggerating? He was killing? He was joking in an official document, when he used the word "killing"? But in order to test the worthiness of their claim, we should look at the converse. Apply that to a defendant or an accused. If, for example, in the Croat intercept, instead of the word "selekcija" "selection" was used, the person said "liquidation," what would this Court do to me, as an officer of the Court, if I argued on the same principles that the Prosecution does, he didn't mean it, he was joking, it's somehow distorted, or that he was probably not -- probably trying just to sympathise or get some credit from his bosses? This honourable Chamber would laugh us and laugh me out of this courtroom and out of the Hague. That's the double standard that the Prosecution wishes to utilise, and that's the double standard that I think should not be allowed. If they want you to believe that Vasic was not involved, if they want you to believe that Vasic did not mean what he said, they simply have the recourse. He was here for a week, waiting to testify. They withdrew him, with very little in terms of an explanation. He's the one witness who may have, although I doubt it very seriously, corroborated some of the nonsensical evidence that we've seen with respect to Mr. Deronjic and whether there was a meeting with Mr. Beara or not in Bratunac in the SDS offices. They don't call that evidence because that evidence doesn't support their case. They don't call people like Malinic and the interpreter and Theo Lutke because there is doubt and flaws in what Mr. Egbers said with respect to Beara's presence. The Prosecution, in its closing remarks, probably regurgitated its brief and highlighted that there were 14 witnesses. As expected and as I've stated, they've chosen quantity over quality. Let it be -- since I'm moving to the issue of specific witnesses, I want to say this to the Court and to the Prosecution: Let there be no doubt that I would prefer one Milan Kerkez over 100 of their Momir Nikolics. Let there be no doubt I would prefer Svetlana Gavrilovic and Mira Cekic over hundreds of Deronjics and Nikolics and Vasics, and PW-161, or, for that matter, anyone from Bratunac. The first witness that the Prosecution uses in their brief to highlight or claim that Ljubisa Beara was involved in any of the actions relating to Srebrenica and Zepa appears on paragraph 2187 and then on paragraphs 2203, 2204, and 2205. In order to be fair and thorough, we must dissect the evidence of each witness and then determine whether that witness should be considered credible and worthy. The OTP relies on one witness, and only one witness, to claim that Ljubisa Beara was at the IKM in Pribicevac. This single witness and his faulty recollection was not confirmed by any other witness. It was not confirmed by any other documents, or any other intercepts, or even the infamous Zvornik Brigade duty officer log-book. Others have testified in this courtroom regarding the IKM in Pribicevac. Others have testified who was present with Krstic at the IKM Pribicevac. Prosecution witnesses testified in that regard. If they believed Bosko Momcilovic, they could have gotten corroborating evidence from other people who were present when Mr. Momcilovic claims he saw Mr. Beara. There is no corroboration from either other witnesses who were present, such as PW-162, such as Mr. Deronjic, such as Defence witness Miljenko Jevdjevic. There's no record of any source to substantiate or corroborate this claim. This witness stands alone with respect to this date, but this witness, like nine others in their -- on their list of 14, is not alone, when you look at the common denominator that there is no corroboration for his evidence, there's no support for it either in the documents, the intercepts, or anywhere else. Look at Butler and what he says with respect to Mr. Beara's whereabouts. It's the Prosecution's military analyst. Certainly, he wouldn't have lied with respect to whether or not Beara was present at the IKM Pribicevac if there was any -- any reasonable source of information to suggest that Beara was present there. He was not, and therefore the Court should not consider this evidence, standing alone, without corroboration, to support the fact or the claim that the Prosecution is offering. If that isn't enough, look at the unrebutted testimony of the Defence witness, who said, and that's Ljuban Mrkovic. We have his intercept. It's reflected on July 10th, that he states that Ljubisa Beara was at the Sarajevo Romanija Corps for four or five days and that Ljubisa Beara afterwards told him that he was going to the Krajina region. On the 10th, he's saying this on the intercept. When he testified, it was unrebutted. Bozo Momcilovic's uncorroborated and unsubstantiated and erroneous recollection cannot be given any weight whatsoever. No records, no video, no documents, and no other witness support his claim. If the Court recalls, there was one other witness who gave testimony, and that was a person by the name of Dragoslav Trisic. Dragoslav Trisic, I think, told the Court uniquely what the problem is with these recollections. Initially, he claimed, surprisingly to both the Prosecution and the Defence, in an interview, not in court, that he thought he may have seen Mr. Beara at Potocari. Simply not true. The Prosecution knew it, never argues it, doesn't argue it, because they know it's not true. During his testimony, he explained that he did, in a prior interview, mention him because he felt pressured. He felt pressured to just name everyone and anyone that he knew. He knew that Mr. Beara was indicted, so he just threw him in a vacuum of people that may or may not have been present. With all due respect, there is no credible evidence whatsoever that Mr. Beara was either in Potocari -- there's no evidence of that, and there's certainly no credible evidence that Mr. Beara was at the IKM in Pribicevac. Momcilovic, also I think if you look closely at his testimony, as opposed to lumping him in the 14 that purportedly saw him, he lied under oath. He said that, In 1995-1996, I saw Mr. Beara on television, in order to substantiate his claim. Mr. Beara was not on television. That was verified by the Prosecution, themselves, when they cross-examined Professor Wagenaar. Finally, with respect to Mr. Momcilovic, who was he, what kind of a witness was he? He was a character witness for Momir Nikolic, someone that the Prosecution, themselves, suggest has not only provided half-truths and lies, but it's someone who came into this courtroom during his sentencing and provided character witness testimony for Momir Nikolic. Enough said on the first witness. The next group of witnesses the Prosecution wants to claim, because they want to enhance their case and say that Beara was in Bratunac from the 10th through the 12th of July, 1995, they identify four witnesses; Zlatan Celanovic, PW-161, respectfully Mr. Borovcanin, and - I've got to get this right again - PW-138. When you view this evidence, they utilise and rely on these witnesses for other aspects of their case, not just the 10th through the 12th. But when you view these individuals, as we're about to, I think the Court will find that they are not credible and not worthy of being given any weight to their testimony. With respect to Zlatan Celanovic, the first and most -- and perhaps the impressive issue with him is that the Prosecution acknowledged and puts forth immediately that Zlatan Celanovic is terrible with dates, cannot remember or recall specifically the date of any meeting or anything that happened. The transcript, at page 6627, the Prosecution asks the following question: "Q. And I want to go to the time of about the fall of the Srebrenica enclave. Now, I know you've testified before that you weren't real good with dates; is that right? "A. That's correct." Zlatan Celanovic, if you view his testimony carefully, clearly did not see Ljubisa Beara from the 10th through the 12th, at least until the evening, as he later claimed, of July 1995 in Bratunac. He admits he's not good with dates. He's vague when he met Beara. How could you get it wrong, whether you met someone in the morning or in the evening? I could certainly understand someone saying, It was mid-afternoon, or early evening, or late afternoon. How do you get it so diametrically different from, I think it was either the evening of the 12th or the morning of the 13th? This meeting, like many meetings with purportedly Mr. Beara, were "mano y mano." Never was there a third part, with the exception of Egbers. These people have these secret meetings in the middle of town in offices that don't belong to military, in places where secretaries see people coming in and out, and there's supposedly military policemen at the door, unknown people sitting in the conference room who happen to be colonels and lieutenant-colonels, never identified; but yet the only person that comes and testifies is one individual who claims to have seen Beara. There's no record to support this claimed meeting with Zlatan Celanovic. There's no other human being who testified that they saw Zlatan Celanovic with Mr. Beara. How could there be a record of the meeting between Zlatan Celanovic and Mr. Beara? We can draw from our own personal experiences, and if, as the Prosecution claims, that Mr. Beara gave an order to Zlatan Celanovic that he needs to interrogate and he needs to investigate, and Mr. Celanovic does interrogate and investigate certain individuals, you would expect to find, in some of his records or in some of his paperwork, that he was instructed or ordered or asked or requested by Ljubisa Beara to do any of these things. The Prosecution is relatively angry and upset because if we accept the proposition that Zlatan Celanovic is credible, although he stands alone, with no documents supporting his version, Butler acknowledges there was nothing illegal or improper with respect to the requests made at that time on the evening of July 12th, 1995, to interrogate, to investigate. They believe Zlatan Celanovic when he claims that he saw Ljubisa Beara on the 12th, in the evening, in Bratunac, all alone, but they do not believe him as to the perfectly legal discussion that Celanovic claims he had. In that regard, Mr. Vanderpuye and the Prosecution say, Mr. Beara was cunning, he was cunning. Where's the proof of that? Isn't that manipulation? Isn't that distortion? What is the basis of making a claim like that? None. If this honourable Trial Chamber accepts Zlatan Celanovic's testimony, the only time he would have been able to see Ljubisa Beara was on the 12th of July, 1995, in the evening, and you respectfully must accept at face value what Celanovic claims Beara purportedly said to him. You cannot accept the Prosecution's baseless version that this was a cunning man trying to deliberately deceive everyone with respect to the work that was purportedly at hand. Celanovic, indeed, says that the interrogation process proceeded and that Beara said these individuals would be transported to Kladanj. Celanovic also confirms that he spoke to another individual, a bus driver, who also told him that the individuals would be transported to Kladanj. I refer the Court to the transcript at pages 6631 through 6632, and also at 6641. The second witness that the Prosecution relies on to try to prove or establish that Ljubisa Beara was present in Bratunac is an accused, Mr. Ljubomir Borovcanin. And with the highest of respect to Mr. Borovcanin, I don't have a case against him and I'm not trying to prove a case against him. Last Friday -- when you view this evidence, the Court allowed it in, I need not remind you what the rules of evidence are and what weight you should give evidence that we, Mr. Beara's Defence team, did not have an opportunity to closely scrutinise and cross-examine, but look at what the Prosecution told you on the 4th of September, 2009, with respect to that interview statement. With all due respect to Mr. Borovcanin, the Prosecution said: "Look at his false statement." "He is lying to me." "There is radical changes from the statement to what's in the brief." Wait, let me get this straight. The Prosecution wants to use Mr. Borovcanin's statement against us, but yet they're telling this Court that he lied, that it's a false statement, that there's radical changes to it? Those concepts, respectfully to Mr. Vanderpuye, do not coexist. PW-138, which is a third witness that the Prosecution uses to support their claim of the 14, in his testimony the OTP is relying to establish Beara's presence again in Bratunac from the 10th through the 12th of July, 1995, but let's take a refreshingly honest and closer look at what he actually said. If we examine transcript page 3802 through 3803, we'll find the following passage, quote -- question by the Prosecution. "Q. So let's take Colonel Beara, for example. Can you tell us whether you know whether he was in the area of Bratunac before the fall of the enclave?" Answer by PW-138: "I've just told you that I cannot -- that I really cannot say whether he," they're referring to Beara in parentheses I place, "was there before the fall of the enclave or not." Further, PW-138 says at transcript page 3803, line 16: "It's all mixed up in my mind." "I'm not sure whether I saw Mr. Beara." "It's all mixed up in my mind." The Prosecution abandons this witness as to a charge of reburial with Mr. Beara, and yet they now want to tell this Court that you should rely on his testimony. We further test this witness's credibility by virtue of the fact that no one has been brought in to corroborate his claim, no records exist, and no intercepts were ever disclosed which would remotely support such a claim. It does speak volumes to the Prosecution that they abandoned PW-138. It does speak volumes as to how they view his recollection, his testimony, as well as his credibility. Relying on a witness such as PW-138, who cannot recall anything with specificity, and admits that he is mixed up, and acknowledges he is uncertain, would be, as Mr. Vanderpuye shared with us, "valueless." The next witness, PW-161, perhaps, but I think certainly, one of the least credible witnesses that this Court has been asked to evaluate. It's clear that with respect to PW-161, that he is inconsistent with his interviews -- his prior interviews with Investigator Ruez, and you can find that quickly and briefly both in our brief, but also I'll provide a cite, which is 9419 and 9420, page number. This witness was called as a Defence witness in the Blagojevic case in order to support a ridiculous claim of parallel chain of command. This witness was brought in the Blagojevic case to support that Mr. Blagojevic was not present or not at Bratunac and did not give orders. This witness, however, when asked whether he can share with us how many times he met with the Blagojevic Defence, couldn't remember, not sure. This witness and his selective memories should be rejected by the Trial Chamber. He acknowledged at that time that he, indeed, gave four or five different versions. This witness also claimed that he did not see Momir Nikolic at that time in Bratunac. If Momir Nikolic is right and he sees Mr. Beara in the centre of town, and from my understanding there's only one road that leads to that centre of town, on any given day, how could this witness, with any credibility, stand before this Court and tell you he never saw Momir Nikolic? He also, this witness, PW-161, claims he didn't see Ljubislav Simic. Here's an individual who worked and coordinated in 1992 with Deronjic, was involved and connected with the killings and the murders that occurred in Glogova and the Bratunac area in 1992. He now comes into this courtroom and tells us that he did not see any of the principle perpetrators of the crimes that occurred in Bratunac in 1992 or 1995? Look carefully at PW-161's testimony. He had a meeting at the Restaurant Jasen. He claims, with Mr. Borovcanin, but also with Miroslav Deronjic, he tells us it was soon after the Kravica killings. Here's what PW-161 said when asked if he remembered anything about that meeting and about the incident that occurred at Kravica, as the question was posed to him. The question referenced "incident at Kravica." He says at transcript page 9364, specifically lines 20 through 21: "It was discussed that evening, but I truly don't remember what Miroslav said, what Borovcanin said, what I said. We talked a lot." This witness that the Prosecution is relying on, who said that he doesn't remember what was discussed after a horrific massacre, after killings were completed at Kravica, he has the audacity to come into court and tell us he doesn't remember what was discussed? This witness, who was in charge, by virtue of his capacity and employment, with digging and obtaining machines, both in 1992 as well as in 1995, realised how deep he was with respect to his criminal culpability and his criminal responsibility. He had no way out. He had to claim that someone else ordered him to do the digging at Glogova. Again, with most if not all of the Prosecution's 14 witnesses, this witness is not corroborated by any other witness. He also sees Beara, mysteriously, alone. He does say, There were two other VRS officers in the room, one a colonel, one a lieutenant-colonel. He claims Beara was in the room. He tells you, conveniently, that he doesn't remember the other two individuals' names. He tells you that when he came into the SDS offices, Deronjic was not there. He passes the secretary, as we know her name now is Mirna Nikolic. He doesn't check in with her, she doesn't make a record of it. There's no evidence to support his claim. He stands alone with respect to his claim that he saw Beara that evening. He does not stand alone with respect to the evidence the Prosecution is bringing against Beara. He, as others like Zlatan Celanovic, like Egbers, like Bozo Momcilovic, all have this unique quality. They all see Mr. Beara alone, in the middle of town, with many people passing, with thousands of people in buses. They're the only ones who see him? No support whatsoever. No MUP records, no records from the civilian authorities that Mr. -- that PW-161 reports to, to simply state, I was asked, I was requested, I was ordered, I had a meeting with this individual. No evidence of that at all. Further, when you evaluate PW-161 and his testimony, you have to view the evidence of one other individual, Momir Nikolic. Momir Nikolic either had a reawakening or he came to his senses to tell, in part, the truth as it relates to this plan, to this lie, to shift the responsibility of the killings in Kravica and the burial at Glogova to Mr. Beara. Momir Nikolic, in his testimony on page 33128, acknowledged to the Prosecution that PW-161 lied about the alleged Beara involvement in Glogova. I asked Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Vanderpuye, in particular, although Mr. Nicholls, with all due respect, is the one who interviewed him and obtained that information initially for us, Why didn't you follow up with PW-161? Here's a lead, here's a witness that you had on your list, a witness you entered into a plea agreement, a witness who now is saying something different than the witness that you brought forth into court. Are we not owed that obligation? Is it not their duty to be fair and thorough? Is it not their duty to bring forth at least some truth in this courtroom as it may relate to an accused? PW-161 was involved with the 1992 Glogova killing and burial. PW-161 was similarly involved at least in the burial in Glogova relating to the Kravica warehouse killings. PW-161 had a tight-knit group of individuals whom he could trust and perpetrate -- and perpetuate a false claim, a claim that he thinks will somehow absolve him of responsibility. His evidence was not only contradicted by Momir Nikolic; his evidence was inconsistent with other statements he, himself, had given. His evidence was not corroborated by anyone or anything. This is the witness that can be coined as deliberately deceptive or cunning, but certainly not Mr. Beara. Moving along on the next group of witnesses that the Prosecution offered in this case, relates to the evening of the 13th and 14th of July, 1995. There are four witnesses that they utilise to support their claim, two of which we've already touched upon. That would be Mr. Borovcanin as well as PW-161. Who is left? Two individuals who have pled guilty, two individuals who acknowledge and admit that they were involved in war crimes in former Yugoslavia. One individual, Miroslav Deronjic, who acknowledged his involvement in the crimes against the Bosnian Muslims in Bratunac and Glogova in 1992, and Momir Nikolic who I think still, although it was unclear from some of his testimony, was involved in the tragedy that occurred to the Srebrenica enclave and the people that made their way through Bratunac and through Zvornik. Those are the four individuals that they rely on. Mr. Vanderpuye was quite clever in mocking or trying to mock the Defence and say, Was someone walking around carrying a suit or a mask of Mr. Beara? No, that's not our defence. Our defence is: When you dissect the evidence fairly and thoroughly, you will find that the evidence the Prosecution stands on has no foundation and should not be accepted, and given no weight. The cunningness and deliberate deception does intertwine with Momir Nikolic and Miroslav Deronjic. However, they couldn't even get their stories straight. Although they are in-laws, related, their testimony between themselves was inconsistent, contradictory, unsubstantiated by others, was not confirmed by records, intercepts, or other data. Mr. Nikolic, the self-admitted liar. He told us he lied about critical issues. He told us he had previously lied about his involvement in Sandici as well as his involvement in the Kravica warehouse. The Prosecution is really relying on that evidence? He admits that he lied, along with PW-161, when they tried to include, shift, and blame Mr. Beara for the killings and burial relating to Kravica and Glogova. He admitted it. We do not, and we respectfully ask you not to accept Mr. Nikolic's false, contrived evidence, and suggest that you reject the same. Deronjic's story does not coincide with Mr. Nikolic's. It can't, because a lie will ultimately be unravelled. Deronjic's story about the alleged meeting in the SDS offices with Beara. Mr. Deronjic passed away during the start of this trial. We did not have an opportunity to cross-examine him. That evidence, much to our disappointment, was nonetheless introduced. There was no evidence to substantiate or corroborate, from a credible source, Mr. Deronjic's view or recollection of the events as they may have occurred specifically relating to Mr. Beara. What the Prosecution could have done was, at the very least, bring forth Mr. Vasic, as I've previously stated, if they wanted to, if they truly believed anything that Mr. Deronjic had said. Mr. Deronjic, just like Momir Nikolic, is a self-admitted liar. We've highlighted for you and we've taken an enormous amount of time in our brief showing you how other people viewed Mr. Deronjic's testimony and recollection, but in order to highlight some of those we can take a closer look and review. Mr. Deronjic's statements and credibility, in my view, can best be described as follows: The forensic value of his statements and testimonies is extremely limited. Not one of the Trial Chambers which heard from Deronjic were satisfied that he was credible or reliable. For example, the Appeals Chamber in Krstic, while analysing Deronjic's testimony, cautioned -- cautioned to everyone, because they knew and had the wisdom that the Prosecution may use Mr. Deronjic's testimony in other cases, they cautioned and said, We "hesitate to base any decision on Mr. Deronjic's testimony without having corroborating evidence." I see that it may be close to the time. I'm not sure if I'd be allowed just to maybe finish with Mr. Deronjic or if the Court is pressed for time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, not at all. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. A closer review of any evidence offered by Deronjic reveals that his statements are not only not fully correct. It is difficult to number the times Deronjic admitted that his previous statements were deliberately not true. The Court has also found in other instances that the details of his statement cannot be taken as true, that he gave false testimony, that he was not truthful in prior instances. Deronjic's testimony should be rejected in its entirety. I have a question for the Prosecution. I wrote these things in our trial brief. Why didn't they reconcile it with the Court? Why do they stand there, proud as a peacock, to tell us, We have 14 witnesses that claim that Beara was there from the 10th through the 16th? Let's dissect it. Their obligation, and it is mine, when they ignore my evidence, to tell them they've ignored it, they could have and they should have told the Court how they truly view Mr. Deronjic's testimony, despite the fact that we didn't have an opportunity to cross-examine him. The only thing that Deronjic may have said that was remotely true was when he claimed, on P3139 - that's the exhibit number - page 119-120, when he was interviewed with the Prosecution and talked to them, he told them, In giving now my second or third interview, I've prepared better. Of course, he doesn't mention, as uniquely, no other witnesses mention Mr. Beara until well after the Krstic case, but this witness, in particular, says to the Prosecution that he's consulted or he's "used some friendly connections" to recreate the chronology of the events? Unsurprisingly, those connections and those people he consulted were the people that he met with in order to perpetuate his lie as to who was ultimately responsible. We're grateful for the intercept that shows Deronjic discussing with former President Karadzic what should be done with the POWs. Does that not indicate Deronjic's involvement? Does the fact that he was appointed to the position that he was clearly reveal that he was responsible for those POWs? Look at the timing of that intercept. At 2010 hours, July 13th, and it's Exhibit P1149, it's immediately prior to this -- or not immediately; it's prior to this purported meeting with Mr. Beara. No mention by Karadzic that he will send him a secret source to inform him what to do with the POWs. No mention in that intercept or any data that Karadzic will send a messenger, or a courier, or an individual to tell Mr. Deronjic what to do with the POWs. Karadzic, through an interpreter, simply tells him what to do, Place them in the warehouse, you know what to do. Deronjic's testimony in this regard, if you look at what he said on the 8th and 9th of July, when he met with Karadzic, that he was already instructed by Karadzic to kill the Muslims, he was already instructed by Karadzic to apply the Western Slavonia method. How do you reconcile now his purported claim that Mr. Beara comes to his office at midnight or at 1.00 in the morning? Simply put, he made it up. He lied in order to shift the responsibility that he had, to shift his involvement from the crimes that were committed and were about to be committed to someone else. How do we explain -- and I'm shocked that I didn't hear it from the Prosecution. How do we -- how do they not reconcile that Deronjic doesn't want the individuals in Bratunac, but purportedly Beara comes in and sees him and says, I want to move the individuals, and they get into this mysterious, heated debate and discussion? Why would it be heated? Deronjic supposedly wants them out, Beara allegedly is asking to move them. There should be no debate. The point is that their lie was uncovered, in part. The point is that their lie cannot hold muster. The point is that there is no evidence to corroborate or substantiate by any other individual that Mr. Beara was present on either the 13th or 14th of July. It might be -- and I appreciate the additional time past the hour. I do have a couple more comments on Mr. Deronjic, but I think it's a good place to stop, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll have a 25-minute break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours. We left off discussing briefly the evidence that was proffered by the Prosecution in connection with Mr. Deronjic. They don't ever reconcile for us, quite candidly, the fact that Mr. Deronjic claimed that he got instructions from Karadzic. Although they were pretty wild in some accusations and inferences that they made, I can probably be certain that they will try to use that evidence in other cases before this Tribunal, but they should reconcile that if it's true that Karadzic gave Mr. Deronjic instructions on the 8th and 9th of July, 1995, to kill the POWs from Srebrenica, it's clear, then, that there was no need for Karadzic to send this purported messenger, courier, or person to give Mr. Deronjic the same information, which is what I think they're saying, in a nutshell. At the end of the day, the Prosecution cannot, certainly, with all due respect, rely on Deronjic's testimony with respect to Mr. Beara for a number of reasons. They know and respect the law of this Tribunal; I'm confident of that. They know that there should not be, at any instance, evidence that is tainted, replete with lies, false innuendos, to be brought forth against a witness. They know the penalty for perjured testimony. But what I don't understand and what they haven't reconciled for me is: How and why do they rely on that testimony? The law is clear that Deronjic's testimony, given that it is asserted against an accused, not subject to cross-examination, they know what the Appellate Court and Trial Chamber has said about Deronjic; essentially, that his testimony is not credible, should not be relied upon without any corroborative evidence, both testimonial or documentary. They know the intercept of the 13th of July, P1149, at 2010 hours. Having all that, they don't reconcile for us how and why they think he's credible and reliable and whether you should give that witness any weight. Their silence, perhaps as others have said, may be deafening, but in this instance their silence with respect to Mr. Deronjic is a clear indication that they, likewise, see and appreciate the fact that Deronjic's testimony is simply a lie. No other witnesses, up to this point, the 13th of July, have been brought forth by the Prosecution, so logically that takes us to the next day, the 14th of July, 1995. Again, Mr. Vanderpuye uses a standard to claim that Milan Kerkez, Mira Cekic, and Svetlana Gavrilovic, that you should scrutinise their testimony carefully, that you should, if they make an inconsistent statement or an implausible statement, reject it in its entirety. I repeat what I've said earlier. I'll accept that standard, so long as it applies to all the witnesses that the Prosecution brought forth. If there is an inconsistency and there is no corroboration, or there is evidence to the contrary, that evidence should be rejected as well. In a nutshell, on the 14th of July the Prosecution provides you with three witnesses that they claim support that Ljubisa Beara was, of all places, in Zvornik, in Bratunac, and Nova Kasaba in that order. If you carefully, as I know you will, review that evidence, you will find that that timeline is not only implausible, but impossible. The first witness that the Prosecution relies on, Milorad Bircakovic, his testimony was rebutted, his testimony was contradicted by the Prosecution evidence with respect to his travel logs. They, themselves, also indicate that it is not possible, the evidence that they disclose to us at P296. That travel log reveals that he did not go from the headquarters to an IKM. That evidence shows the time, the date, five people that he was travelling with at that time. Not only do the documents contradict Milorad Bircakovic, who initially claimed that he brought Drago Nikolic from the IKM to the headquarters and that he claimed that he saw Beara at the Zvornik headquarters. What's important in this analysis is to review the timing of when it occurred. And, again, he states that it was 8.00, 8.30, to be fair to the Prosecution. He tells us how long the meeting purportedly took place. He tells us how long it took him to go from Zvornik Brigade headquarters to the IKM and back. He then tells us when they purportedly left. Interestingly, Witness PW-162 seems to be having a meeting alone, with no one else to support it, with Mr. Beara in Bratunac at or approximately the same time, 9.00, 9.30. It's impossible to reconcile these witnesses without taking them together. You've been to the site. You know how long it would have taken you to travel there under better condition. I dare say that at the time that the Prosecution alleges, the 14th of July, that the conditions did not allow for quicker travel to get from one place to another within such a short period of time. What's complicated about the Prosecution's theory is that they add another factor. Although Mr. Butler thought that Vincent Egbers saw Beara on the 13th or 12th, by virtue of his testimony, it is now pretty clear - and I can give the Court the cite, if it wishes - that, in fact, Egbers claims to have seen Mr. Beara on the 14th, and that's what's claimed by the Prosecution, again in the morning. In a nutshell, their case on the 14th of July, 1995, is that Beara was in three different places at or approximately the same time, with three separate individuals, but, according to the Prosecution, we do not have corroborating evidence for any of those three instances. With respect to PW-162, who claims that he saw Beara in the morning of July 14th, 1995, we need only look at what he said at page 9627 and 9628, where he cannot recognise Beara. Our brief goes into greater detail at paragraph 116 in that regard. PW-162 is the individual that Deronjic spoke about when he said that he had these close connections and that he could reinvent the chronology of events. PW-162 was troubled by the fact that we knew, during his testimony, that he had spoken with Deronjic. He first seemed to deny it. Then he recalled it. Then he simply dismissed it. PW-162 is the individual who claimed that when he went to see Beara at the SDS offices, that the secretary called him in to visit with Beara. There's no secretary or evidence from a secretary to confirm such a claim. There's no record of the SDS offices to support that these meetings ever took place, much less at the SDS offices. The circumstances of the meeting that Witness PW-162 gave evidence on are suspect as well. He claims that Beara brought him to the SDS president -- president's offices to talk to another colonel and a lieutenant-colonel, who again, like PW-161, they don't know who those other individuals are. They can't remember. In fact, during their bald-faced lie, they said, Those individuals were never introduced to us. These unknown sources by these witnesses, both PW-161 and 162, clearly reveal the lies in their stories. PW-162, unlike PW-161, says that Beara was not in the office with the two other individuals, but that he just merely brought him in the office and stayed outside. PW-162 and 161, although in their clever attempt to implicate others, clearly mixed up their story. They both wanted to have the same story so that a prosecutor, an investigator, or perhaps even a judge would believe that such a meeting took place. It did not. There's no evidence to support either the claim of PW-161, 162, or Milorad Bircakovic that would be considered independent or credible that this Court would be able to rely upon. Given the fact that there's no corroborating evidence, given the fact that there's no testimony from other individuals to support, to confirm, or even to mildly recollect similar instances, I suggest, with all due respect, that the Court reject the testimony in its entirety of PW-161 and 162. That leaves us with Mr. Egbers. My comments earlier about Mr. Egbers obviously still hold true, as does of our brief. Mr. Egbers is unique and presents a unique problem for the Defence. He seemed, and I'm sure he was, genuine in his comments that he gave. However, in a criminal proceeding, where the Prosecution, with all due respect, is seeking a life sentence, I respectfully believe more is required, more than just the testimony of one individual who seems genuine, who seems independent. The Prosecution had the wherewithal, had the knowledge, and certainly has the experience to have brought forth to this courtroom corroborating evidence as it relates to Mr. Egbers. Instead, what do they offer you? They offer you an aerial shot to show that there were, indeed, Bosnian Muslims, POWs, in Nova Kasaba. I don't think we're disputing that. I think we're disputing that it was actually Mr. Beara at Nova Kasaba. The Honourable Judge Kwon asked me, during this case, early in the case, when Egbers testified, What's your position? Unlike the Prosecution, when asked questions, I responded directly. I could have, and some advocates suggest, that I should have merely said, Honourable Judge Kwon, I don't have the burden of proof, I don't need to answer that question. They have to prove that Mr. Beara was there. They easily could have proved that, chose not to. That inference, the fact that they refused to call Zoran Malinic, that they refused to call the interpreter, Nebojsa, the fact that the Prosecution failed to call Theo Lutke to substantiate or corroborate Mr. Egbers, should be examined very closely. If those individuals, any three of them, remembered, recalled, or knew that Mr. Beara was there, we would have seen those three individuals. The inference is clear. Those individuals did not and do not support Mr. Egbers on this point. Quickly, to turn to Witness PW-104 that the Prosecution alleges in their list of 14 witnesses that purportedly saw Mr. Beara, this witness also claimed that Mr. Beara was at the Zvornik Brigade headquarters on the 14th of July, in the evening. With respect to his testimony, I think once you review it carefully and cautiously, you'll find that it's implausible. He was a local civilian who worked with Deronjic and the Bratunac personnel, both in 1992, through his relations through other individuals who were elected office in Zvornik. With this witness, as with ten other witnesses that the Prosecution has brought forth with respect to the presence and identity of Mr. Beara, there is no corroboration. This witness, in particular, says that he cannot recall which officers of the Zvornik Brigade were present when he met with Beara. He cannot recall how many persons were present during this purported meeting. Likewise, he could not confirm the identity of Beara. Look closely, in his admitted statements, and I think you'll find the motivation that this person needed to shift the responsibility and blame to someone like Beara. Look closely at the records in his case, and you'll find in his statement that (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: (redacted), an individual who was also assisting in transporting Bosnian Muslims from Bratunac to various places. That's his motivation. This witness was uncorroborated by any evidence, by any witness, and clearly when you review his testimony, you'll find it to be implausible and impossible. We do have one other individual on the 14th of July, 1995, and that's Marko Milosevic. He's, as we know, the deputy commander of the Zvornik Brigade 6th Battalion. Now, here's an individual who wanted to try to tell us that he did have corroborating evidence with his deputy, of all people, Ostoja Stanisic. Together, these individuals want you to believe that near or around the Petkovci school, which was close, I thought he said that when he claimed to have seen Beara, he walked over to the school, prisoners were held at that school, of no concern to Mr. Stanisic or to Mr. Milosevic, apparently, he walked there and simply conveyed a message to Mr. Beara. How plausible is that? How realistic is that, that a deputy commander and a commander of the 6th Battalion, knowing, seeing, appreciating the situation, would not have reported it to someone, would not have recorded it anywhere? If it's true that Beara was there, all they had to do was write it in their log-book. It's a positive thing for them to say, Hey, look, bad things are happening five seconds away from us or five minutes from where we're at. Other people are there. We don't want to get involved in it. Instead, they tell you that when they came back to the command, they heard shots. They knew what was going on. I challenged Mr. Ostoja Stanisic and said that he was involved in the killings and his men were involved in the killings. He took it rather personally, as he should have. It is not possible for a commander or a deputy commander, such as Marko Milosevic, to say with any credibility that they knew what was going on at Petkovci school, that they went to Petkovci school, saw Beara, but didn't record that anywhere. It's not plausible, their story. You heard, although it was not revealed to us from the Prosecution, these two individuals were interviewed by the Prosecution on the same day. They travelled together for three or four hours in the car. Before they meet with the Prosecutor of the ICTY to discuss Srebrenica and their involvement, they again lied and said, We really didn't discuss the events. We talked about various things, but we didn't want to discuss it. They weren't serious. It's not plausible, it's not possible, that in a three-hour ride, if it's true that they saw Mr. Beara and if it's true that they knew that there were POWs in the Petkovci school, it's not plausible that they didn't discuss it on the car ride to visit with the Prosecutor in the first interview. They concocted the story. They've made it up in order to shift the responsibility, because they knew that they were responsible. It was within their zone of responsibility, Petkovci school. The least they could have done and what they should have done, if there is any truth to their claim that Beara was present, was record it. Later, they could use that to try to absolve themselves of responsibility. They didn't do it because they couldn't do it. They knew that Beara was not there. Now, they claim they conveyed a message to Beara. No one else confirms that they saw Beara at Petkovci school, no one else confirms that Beara went back to where Ostoja Stanisic was to make this phone call. Nowhere in the log-book do they write down, Yes, we've given the message to Colonel Beara. I think those log-books are highly suspicious, and I'll address that issue later in my arguments and submissions. There is no doubt that Ostoja Stanisic and Marko Milosevic coordinated their testimony. There is no doubt, that it's impossible to believe, that these two people who are placed in charge of a battalion would have notified others of the circumstances involved in Petkovci, and there's clearly no doubt that if it's even remotely true or possible, that a third party, such as Mr. Beara, was actively engaged in activity at Petkovci, they would have written that down, they would have shared it with others, and they certainly would have been able to use that to absolve them of any responsibility in those crimes. Again, with respect to Marko Milosevic, there is truly no corroborating evidence. There is, what the Prosecution says, some consistency that the record mentions, looking for Beara or convey a message to Beara. However, we are in a criminal trial, and the standard of proof is not that there's consistent evidence; there must be conclusive evidence. Such conclusive evidence does not exist as to any of the purported identities of Mr. Beara and his presence at any of the sites or venues as claimed by the Prosecution. July 15th, 1995, in the evening. The Prosecution's brief relies on one witness in this regard, and that is PW-165. PW-165 spent the entire day that day guarding and watching the POWs at Rocevic school. Upon return to the barracks, someone, again consistent with what they're telling the Court, an unknown person, told PW-165: "Well, the commander had a meeting with Popovic and Beara." This witness's testimony is not only, as Mr. Vanderpuye says, valueless, it is truly worthless in the regard of identity of Mr. Beara. This witness was not corroborated by anyone. This witness doesn't even remember who told him that it was Beara. This witness also claims that on the 15th of July, 1995, when he references the commander, he references Obrenovic. Look at what PW-168 says about Obrenovic. And I know I said that inartfully. Look specifically at that testimony. PW-168 denies being present at that meeting. Look further at PW-168's testimony and examine the OTP brief at paragraph 867, the transcript of PW-168's testimony at 17061, where he clearly says that he never saw Beara from the 12th through the 18th of July. PW-165 also acknowledges and admits that he never saw Beara before or after this incident, or during. He simply says, Some unknown person told me that they were at the barracks. PW-165, as a military policeman from the Zvornik Brigade, clearly would have told us if he had seen Beara at the Rocevic school or anywhere near the Zvornik Brigade on the 15th of July. PW-165 and his testimony are, again, as I've stated, in my view, respectfully, worthless, and no weight should be given to it. The next day, the 16th of July, 1995. Again, the Prosecution relies on solely one witness. We invite you to look at our brief again at page 130, paragraph 424, with respect to the analysis of Mr. Slavko Peric. But quickly to share with you what he said, Peric admitted, under oath, that he "cannot say with any certainty" that the person he purportedly saw was Beara; transcript 11411, May 112007. He told the Court, being subject to perjury charges: "I cannot say with any certainty." The Prosecution chose to ignore that evidence. They chose not to try to reconcile it for the Court, and they simply stand by his inconsistent version when and if he actually saw Mr. Beara. Again, with this witness, Slavko Peric, as with PW-165, 161, 162, Bosko Momcilovic, and others that I've highlighted, there is no corroborating evidence to support or to be able to even give any weight to the testimony of this person who claims to have seen Beara on the 16th of July, 1995. Now, the 16th of July, 1995, seems to be a good transition for us to look at some of the intercepts. But before we do that, I just want to highlight, again, of the 14 witnesses that the Prosecution claims that they support that Beara was present at or around Bratunac or Zvornik, 10 of them were not corroborated, 10 of them had no records to support what they were claiming, 10 of them saw -- heard from unknown sources, were unfamiliar with Mr. Beara, as described by Professor Wagenaar in his testimony. But the Prosecution, I think, respectfully, missed the point of Professor Wagenaar. They seem, in their brief, to embrace and endorse his view. All Professor Wagenaar was trying to tell us is that there is a clear methodology and a way in which, if you're going to have identification evidence, that there's a procedure as to how you should follow it. We did spend an awful lot of time going over the characteristics of Mr. Beara. They were clear, they were distinct. The witnesses' testimony in that regard were also inconsistent, and I ask and invite the Court to review that when determining whether any weight should be given to these witnesses. If 10 out of the 14 witnesses had no corroboration, had no support, or, as the Prosecution called, were either liars or gave false statements, what four are left? The four witnesses that are left, respectfully, are Momir Nikolic, Miroslav Deronjic, PW-161, and Ljubomir Borovcanin. If we exclude Mr. Borovcanin, which I shall, there's three witnesses in this case who claim that they have seen Mr. Beara. And if you add PW-162 to these three witnesses, those four witnesses, examine their testimony closely and you'll find the inconsistency. You'll find not the loop-hole in order to acquit Mr. Beara; you'll find the fairness and thoroughness which is required in these proceedings, that the Prosecution failed to meet their burden of proof beyond the reasonable doubt. Double-check PW-138. Let the Prosecution tell us why they chose to abandon his testimony. Look closely at Zlatan Celanovic and you'll find that Mr. Beara was not, could not have been, and there's no support that he was with him in Bratunac at any time. Is it a coincidence or convenience that the Zvornik Brigade persons who testified had no corroboration, had no support, but yet claimed that Ljubisa Beara was present at certain times? With respect to the 14th, as I've already stated, the timeline makes no sense for an individual to go from Zvornik Brigade headquarters, down through to Bratunac, back up towards Nova Kasaba, within that short period of time. The burden of proof rests with the Prosecution. With all due respect to them, they failed to carry that burden on each and every instance in which they claim Beara was present. Certainly compare and contrast the testimony of our Defence witnesses with that of the Prosecution, but do not let the Prosecutor convince you or anyone that there should be this double standard; that if a witness is inconsistent or cannot recall a date, that as long as it's a Defence witness, you should reject that testimony, but if it is a Prosecution witness, you should embrace it. I am confident that you will not do that. The next issue, as Mr. Butler himself acknowledged and admits, who spent an inordinate amount of time analysing the documents, the evidence, the statements, as a military analyst on behalf of the Prosecution, he told us quite frankly and quite candidly that Mr. Beara was nowhere to be seen from the 17th through the 31st of July, 1995. He told us also that he had no evidence of Mr. Beara from the 1st through approximately the 12th of July, 1995; no statements, no records, no documents to support such a theory. The Prosecution does not reconcile that with the evidence and the position they're taking in their final brief. They simply do what they're accustomed to doing; ignore it, ignore the evidence just like you ignore 2D PW-19. Ignore the evidence, just like you would Jakov Bienenfeld, ignore the evidence just like you would of Zoran Malinic and the others. With respect to Mr. Butler and the Zepa issue and the charges brought forth on Zepa, his testimony, on 20213, highlights the case that the Prosecution claims they have against Beara. The question is as follows: "Q. From the 17th of July until the 31st of July, 1995, what did your analysis find as to the whereabouts of Mr. Beara?" "A. I don't believe we have any intercepts or any other information pertaining to his whereabouts during this period." Subsequently, we asked him: "When did the Zepa operation start and when did it end?" He gives it to us at page 20216, lines 12 through approximately 20, and he offers to us: "Keep it in the proper context, Mr. Ostojic." And I accept it. And then I ask him: "Give us the timeline of when the operation started and when it ended so that we'll know if someone who was not there, who did not know anything about it, had any responsibility." He shares with us: "The civilians were being transported from the Zepa enclave starting the 26th of July, if memory serves." "When did it end, sir?" "I think within two days, three days, the movement was done." "So would that be the 28th or 29th, according to your analysis?" "Yes, sir. I mean, I believe I have the dates in my report. It was not a very large movement process, two days max." I go back to Mr. Butler, and I ask him at the very next page, at 20217: "Q. In fact, am I correct, sir, that there is no evidence whatsoever with respect to Ljubisa Beara involved in the Zepa operation but for the intercepts that we see, purportedly, on the 1st and 2nd of August, 1995?" "A. To my knowledge, that's correct. I'm not aware of any information." I went on, on that page, to ask him about planning, organising, assisting, supervising, even facilitating, although I don't accept the definition given by the Prosecution. I think it remains unclear what they mean by that. With respect to Zepa, the Prosecution, interestingly, in their brief ignore the evidence of Butler and they rely on one witness, PW-109. And they say that this witness, remarkably, remembers that Mr. Beara was supposedly somewhere near the Zepa check-point. Look closely at the evidence of PW-109. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Again, when you assess the credibility and the weight of the witness and the evidence that the Prosecution is required to bring forth, there is no corroboration to this evidence, it is weak, in my opinion, it is not conclusive. This witness could not pin-point the date at all. We know and we acknowledge Mr. Beara's involvement on the 1st of August, 1995, well after the operation ceased to unfold. The Prosecution is trying to put Mr. Beara at the Zepa check-point well before the August 1st, 1995 intercept. They have no proof, no evidence, no corroboration, or no documents, but for one witness, to support that claim. Again, it's not that difficult. If you really believe this, Mr. Prosecutor, there were other people at the check-point. You have evidence, video evidence, of other people at the check-point at certain times. There's no evidence that Mr. Beara was at the check-point during or before the operation, none whatsoever. Fair and thorough is what I would have expected. I don't believe we got it in connection with the witnesses. I don't believe we got it with what they call other evidence to support their position as it relates to Mr. Beara, and that is the intercept evidence. And I'd like to turn to the intercept evidence. And as I briefly shared with you, we ended with the witness on the 16th of July, and in the interests of time and by way of an example, we should look at the 16th of July intercept. I think that it is intercept P1187. And if we could just have that -- thank you. If we could have that placed before the Court. Now, this intercept purports to be a conversation at 1111 hours on the 16th of July, 1995, between Beara, Cerovic and X. They claim that "triage" was a code word for "murder." They don't accept, when Vasic says "liquidate" or "kill," that it means what it says at face value, but they concoct now the word "triage" as being a code word for "murder." Looking at this intercept carefully, as I hope that we would and that you will, who used the word "triage" during this intercept? Here it is. From recollection, it's used four times. All four times, it's used by Cerovic, not Beara. The Prosecution says, as does their expert, Mr. Butler, that there was no triage of POWs that were conducted on July 16th, 1995. Therefore, this must mean, based on their leap of logic, that it must mean to kill. That's not true, and the Prosecution knows it. The other intercept or evidence that you should look at is also P12. Now, P12 -- I'm sorry, P1200. Thank you. I apologise for that. P1200, this intercept is dated the 16th of July, 1995, at 1948 hours. It's between two other participants, discussing vehicles, issues with wounded and injured people. This, surprisingly, intercept is relied upon by the Prosecution to say that others knew, others may have known. This intercept clearly is talking about triage, and the triage of the wounded, and the triage of the sick, and the triage of the people that were left in Bratunac and Potocari -- and Srebrenica, excuse me. But you don't have to take my word for it. It's in the document, on page 2. If you look at that document, on page 2 the word "triage" appears, and it's ERN 009-35916. The 16th of July, 1995, others are discussing triage. Is that enough? I think it's enough to create reasonable doubt. The Prosecution simply ignores it. But look at P2567, if you will. It's also dated the 16th of July, 1995. Now, mind you, the Prosecution is taking the view that there was no triage, that there was no evidence of wounded. P2567, which is a Main Staff document dated the 16th of July, 1995, discusses the coordination between various parties in order to transport approximately 100 people from Potocari and Bratunac to Tuzla. You must view the evidence that the Prosecution claims as it relates to Mr. Beara, the intercept of the 16th of July, 1995, P1187, together with P1200 and P2567 and, respectfully, ask yourselves whether their interpretation of the word "triage" is accurate or correct when used on that date. It is not, and this is just their attempt at an imaginary claim which they so desperately need as it relates to Mr. Beara. Now, we're going to look at a couple other intercepts, and in the interests of time I may skip some, but it's hopefully covered in our brief in detail. If we look at P1130, which is also an intercept that the Prosecution claims identifies Mr. Beara at 1015 hours, it's the intercept between Zoka, Beara, and Lucic. The OTP, in their closing remarks, asked a quizzical question and said, This intercept is hotly contested by the Beara Defence, and I don't see why. I invite you to look at the three copies that you have of P1130. You'll find that in the handwritten copy, nowhere does the word "Beara speaking" appear. All we see is "Beara," somehow magically that appears in the English translation. The typed version speaks for itself, I suppose. Also, the handwritten version and this witness who testified, clearly he said -- during the second half of this document, clearly he said, I want to talk to him, Lucic wanting to talk to Cerovic. This witness, although he was a Prosecution witness, clearly stood by that. Now, the Prosecution's claim is that Beara wanted to talk to Zoka - I said "Cerovic" by mistake, Zoka - that Beara wanted to talk to Zoran Malinic, but it was actually Lucic as recorded by the intercept operator who wanted to talk to Zoka. It was clear in his testimony, and I invite you to look at that testimony again. The next point that's interesting about this P1130, if you look at the first portion that seems to indicate that Beara was one of the speakers, look at the questions that are being asked by, purportedly, Beara. Is this a man who had knowledge? Is this a man who was well informed? Is this a man who knew what was going on at that time, or is it logical to conclude that this person had no idea, had no information? His first question: "Where are they now?" According to the Prosecution's overall case, Beara should already have known, by 1000 hours, where they were. He goes on, attributed to Beara: "And they've been rounded up, disarmed, everything?" How does the Prosecution reconcile that? If Beara had knowledge by the 13th, this intercept that they claim is Beara certainly doesn't corroborate that. He goes on to ask other questions that are attributed to Beara: "And there is someone to guard them?" He goes on: "They're locked up; right?" Finally: "Do you have enough room over there?" Certainly, that individual who was asking those questions did not know, did not have any knowledge, and certainly was not involved in any aspect of either the transportation nor the killing of the Bosnian Muslims. You'll find, on the next page, where Lucic says: "Let me talk to him," which is what I referenced earlier, and I invite you to look at this particular intercept operator's testimony in regard to that issue and how steadfast he was and determined that the Prosecution's theory is incorrect and that Lucic was actually seeking to speak with Zoka. P1144, temporally connected with the prior exhibit, P1130, it's an intercept of the 13th of July, 1995, at 1829 hours. Now, this intercept, interestingly enough, the Prosecution identifies and says the following in their footnote, of all places, 4904, in paragraph 2215 of their brief, with respect to P1144, the Prosecution says the following: "The intercept clearly shows that there were VRS members who were not informed about the murder operation and who were, therefore, concerned about screening the captured Muslim men for possible war crimes. Otherwise, they would go scot-free, i.e., be exchanged." This is at 1829. The Croat intercept that Mr. Beara was captured on, which the Prosecution is exculpatory, identifies a process of selection, of potential or purported war criminals and the transfer of individuals to the Batkovici camp. The Prosecution call that intercept, the Croat intercept, deliberately deceptive. They criticised us for not going further and trying to identify where the intercept came from, who recorded it.
